summary: Describes the Internet X.509 PKI Certificate Management Protocol, with messages for creating and managing X.509v3 certificates. It supports online exchanges between a certification authority and a client. It is a standards-track document, replaced by RFC 9810.

plainLanguage.summary: CMP is the conversation between a certificate authority and the people who want certificates from it. It covers asking for a certificate, proving you hold the matching private key, updating and revoking certificates, and recovering lost keys.

how does cmp prove possession of a private key

subtitle: The online protocol a certificate authority and a client use to create and manage X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: A public key infrastructure needs a way for a certificate authority and its clients to talk online about issuing, updating, revoking and recovering certificates.
tldr.mechanism: CMP defines a set of ASN.1 messages, each with a common header, a body that names the operation and the protection applied to it, and optional extra certificates, plus the procedures that use them.
tldr.outcome: The document was a Proposed Standard until it was obsoleted by RFC 9810, and it is also updated by RFC 6712, RFC 9480 and RFC 9481.

today: RFC 4210 has been obsoleted by RFC 9810, and the metadata also records updates by RFC 6712, RFC 9480 and RFC 9481. It was a Proposed Standard published in September 2005, and it describes the message format and procedures for managing X.509 certificates online.

sections.title: What CMP Is And What Changed
sections.content:
This document describes the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Management Protocol. Protocol messages are defined for X.509v3 certificate creation and management, and CMP provides on-line interactions between PKI components, including an exchange between a certification authority and a client system.

It obsoletes RFC 2510, and it differs from that document in a handful of ways. The PKI management message profile section is split into two appendices, one required and one optional, and some formerly mandatory functionality moves to the optional profile. The message confirmation mechanism has changed substantially. A new polling mechanism is introduced, deprecating the old polling method at the CMP transport level, and the transport protocol issues are moved to a separate document. A new implicit confirmation method is introduced to reduce the number of protocol messages exchanged in a transaction. There are also smaller enhancements and better explanatory text.

The design principle behind the whole document is stated early: the PKI must be structured to be consistent with the types of individuals who must administer it. Giving administrators unbounded choices complicates the software and increases the chance that a subtle mistake by an administrator or a developer leads to a broader compromise, while restricting them with cumbersome mechanisms will cause them not to use the PKI at all.
sections.plainLanguage: CMP is the set of messages a certificate authority and its clients exchange to create and manage certificates. This version replaced RFC 2510 and changed how confirmations and polling work.

sections.title: The PKI Management Model
sections.content:
Three kinds of party take part. The end entity is the entity the certificate is issued to, which may be a person or an application. The certification authority issues the certificate. A registration authority may also be involved. End entities need secure local access to some information, at a minimum their own name and private key and the name of a certification authority.

The operations for which management messages are defined fall into groups. CA establishment covers setting up a new authority, producing initial revocation lists and exporting its public key. End entity initialization covers importing a root CA public key and asking what options a management entity supports. Certification covers everything that results in a new certificate: initial registration and certification, key pair update, certificate update, CA key pair update, cross-certification request and cross-certificate update. A cross-certificate is one in which the subject CA and the issuer CA are different, and the certificate is issued for the subject CA's signing key; it is inter-domain when the two authorities belong to different administrative domains.

Then there are discovery operations, where certificates and revocation lists are published, and recovery operations, used when an end entity has lost its key store. Revocation operations cover an authorized person advising a certification authority of an abnormal situation requiring revocation. On-line protocols are not the only way of doing any of this: every operation also has off-line methods, and the specification does not require the messages to be used. When hardware tokens are involved, many operations can be done as part of delivering the token.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties take part: the person or program that wants a certificate, the authority that issues it, and sometimes a registration authority that checks the request first. Between them they cover getting a first certificate, replacing keys, publishing certificates and revocation lists, and recovering lost keys.

sections.title: Proving You Hold The Private Key
sections.content:
To prevent certain attacks and to let a certification authority or registration authority check that the binding between an end entity and a key pair is real, the operations let an end entity prove that it has possession of the private key matching the public key it wants certified. Each authority is free to choose how to enforce this, out-of-band procedures or in-band messages, since it is a policy matter, but authorities must enforce it by some means. Many operational protocols in use, such as ordinary electronic mail, do not explicitly check the binding, so until protocols that do check it are ubiquitous, the binding can only be assumed to have been checked. If it is not checked, certificates in the Internet PKI end up being somewhat less meaningful.

The method depends on the type of key. For a signature key, the end entity signs a value. For an encryption key, it can either provide the private key to the authority or be required to decrypt a value. That decryption can be direct, where the authority issues a random challenge that must be answered immediately, or indirect, where the authority issues a certificate encrypted for the end entity, which demonstrates its ability to decrypt it in the confirmation message. The specification encourages the indirect method because it needs no extra messages. For a key agreement key, the end entity and the authority must establish a shared secret key.

The specification also allows an end entity to give the proof to a registration authority, which then attests to the certification authority that the proof was received and validated, though some policies may forbid this. A separate section covers how a root CA changes its key pair. The CA protects its new public key using its previous private key and vice versa, which means generating two extra certificate values if certificates are made available through an X.500 directory, for a total of four: OldWithOld, OldWithNew, NewWithOld and NewWithNew. The entities most affected are those that acquired the old CA public key out of band, and they need the new key protected with the old private key only until they acquire the new public key the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a certificate is issued, the applicant has to show it holds the private key that goes with the public key in the certificate. The way it shows this depends on the kind of key: sign something, decrypt something, or agree a shared secret with the authority.

sections.title: The PKI Message Structure
sections.content:
Every message in the protocol has the same shape: a PKIMessage is a header, a body, optional protection bits and optional extra certificates. The header carries information common to many messages, such as addressing and transaction identification. Because the protection is computed over the header and body together, this information is protected too, so no assumption is made that the transport is secure. The body carries the message-specific information and is a choice between 27 alternatives, one for each operation, from an initialization request through to a polling response. The extra certificates field can hold certificates useful to the recipient, for example so that an end entity can verify its own new certificate when the issuing authority is not a root for it; it does not necessarily contain a certification path, so the recipient may have to sort and select from them.

The header holds a protocol version number, fixed at 2 for this version, then the sender and recipient names, an optional message time, the algorithm used to protect the message, optional key identifiers for the sender and recipient, an optional transaction identifier, nonces, free text and general information. If nothing is known about the sender, as in the initialization request where the end entity may not yet know its own name, the sender field must be null and a key identifier must point at the shared secret to use.

When protection is applied it is either a signature or a message authentication code, and the input to the calculation is the DER encoding of the header and body together. A message may deliberately leave out the protection field when protection is applied outside PKIX instead, for example PKCS #7 or the security multiparts of RFC 1847. That is often unsuitable for initial registration or key recovery, because such mechanisms usually assume the end entity already has a certificate or a unique distinguished name, so for those bootstrapping cases the in-protocol protection may be necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CMP message has a header naming the sender, the recipient and the transaction, a body naming the operation, and optionally a signature or a checksum over the first two. It can also carry extra certificates to help the receiver build a path to a root.

sections.title: Mandatory Management Functions And Version Negotiation
sections.content:
A section sets out the functions that all end entity and certification authority or registration authority implementations must be able to provide, although the same results may be achieved by other means. A newly created root CA must produce a self-certificate and a fingerprint of it, so that end entities which acquire the fingerprint securely can verify the certificate and everything in it; the fingerprint travels in the OOBCertHash structure. When a CA updates its key pair it may issue the NewWithNew, NewWithOld and OldWithNew certificates to help existing holders of the old self-signed certificate move securely to the new one, and to help new holders acquire the old one for verifying existing data. Initializing a subordinate CA works like initializing an end entity, except that it must also produce an initial revocation list, and a new CA must produce empty versions of each revocation list before issuing any certificates.

Cross-certification is a one-way operation producing one new cross-certificate, so if certificates are needed in both directions each authority must initiate a turn. The responder's administrator identifies the authority it wants to cross certify and its equipment generates an authorization code, which is passed out of band to the requester's administrator and entered there to start the exchange. The code is turned into a symmetric key that produces message authentication codes on all the messages, or signatures can be used instead if the authorities can retrieve and validate each other's public keys.

Version negotiation lets old and new implementations talk. A client that knows what the server supports sends the highest version both support; one that does not know sends the highest it supports. A server that receives a version it supports must answer in the same version; if the version is higher or lower than it supports, it must return an error message with the unsupportedVersion bit set, using its highest supported version if the received version was higher and its lowest if it was lower. A client that gets such an error with a version it supports may retry the request at that version. Because RFC 2510 had only one version, the document also spells out what happens when an old and a new implementation meet.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists what every implementation has to be able to do: make a root certificate and a fingerprint of it, rotate a root key safely, produce empty revocation lists, and cross-certify with another authority. It also says how a client and a server agree on a protocol version when they do not have the same one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Three points are spelled out. First, when an end entity proves possession of a decryption key it is effectively challenged to decrypt something, in this case its own certificate. Such a scheme could be vulnerable if the holder of the key could be fooled into decrypting an arbitrary challenge and returning the plaintext to an attacker. Other failures would also be needed for the attack to succeed, but future services such as notary or trusted time could be vulnerable, so implementations should be very careful about decrypting arbitrary ciphertext and revealing the recovered plaintext.

Second, exposing a private key to the authority as proof of possession carries some risk, depending on whether that authority can be trusted to handle such material. Implementers are advised to exercise caution in choosing and using this particular mechanism, and where appropriate to have the user explicitly state that they are willing to trust the authority to hold a copy of their private key before revealing it.

Third, a small subgroup attack during a Diffie-Hellman key exchange can be carried out by a malicious end entity that deliberately chooses parameters letting it derive a significant number of bits of the authority's Diffie-Hellman private key during a key archival or recovery operation. Knowing that, it could retrieve the decryption private key of another end entity during that entity's legitimate archival or recovery. Two courses of action avoid this: the authority may generate a fresh Diffie-Hellman key pair for each end entity it interacts with, or it may run a key validation protocol, which this document does not specify. The first option needs no extra protocol exchanges and is therefore the one recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo warns about three traps: a client that will decrypt anything it is asked to, a client that hands over its private key to prove it owns it, and a client that picks Diffie-Hellman parameters to steal the authority's private key.

viz.caption: THE PKI MESSAGE BODY CHOICES (RFC 4210 SECTION 5.1.2)

items.label: Initialization Request
items.desc: Asks what the authority supports.

items.label: Initialization Response
items.desc: The answer to an initialization request.

items.label: Certification Request
items.desc: Asks for a certificate.

items.label: Certification Response
items.desc: Carries the issued certificate.

items.label: PKCS #10 Request
items.desc: A certification request in the older format.

items.label: Proof of possession challenge
items.desc: Asks the end entity to decrypt a value.

items.label: Proof of possession response
items.desc: Carries the decrypted value.

items.label: Key Update Request
items.desc: Asks for a new certificate for a new key pair.

items.label: Key Update Response
items.desc: The answer to a key update request.

items.label: Key Recovery Request
items.desc: Asks to recover backed-up key material.

items.label: Key Recovery Response
items.desc: The answer to a key recovery request.

items.label: Revocation Request
items.desc: Asks for a certificate to be revoked.

items.label: Revocation Response
items.desc: The answer to a revocation request.

items.label: Cross-certification Request
items.desc: Asks another authority to cross-certify.

items.label: Cross-certification Response
items.desc: Carries the new cross-certificate.

items.label: Certificate confirmation
items.desc: Confirms receipt and acceptance of a certificate.

items.label: Confirmation
items.desc: Confirms the transaction.

items.label: General Message
items.desc: Carries general information, such as a status request.

items.label: General Response
items.desc: The answer to a general message.

items.label: Error Message
items.desc: Reports a failure and its reason.

items.label: Polling request
items.desc: Asks whether a transaction has finished.

items.label: Polling response
items.desc: The answer to a polling request.

viz.caption: THREE WARNINGS FROM THE SECURITY SECTION (RFC 4210 SECTION 8)

items.title: Decryption proof
items.text: A client asked to prove it holds a decryption key should be careful about decrypting arbitrary ciphertext and returning the plaintext.

items.title: Handing over the private key
items.text: Showing the private key to the authority as proof of possession carries risk, and the user should be told they are trusting it with a copy.

items.title: Small subgroup attack
items.text: A malicious client can choose Diffie-Hellman parameters that let it work out the authority's private key. The authority should generate a fresh key pair for each end entity.
